## ▸ User [127]

what does heuristic mean ; we are only using the seed.npz ; right?

### Claude [127]

Good question to pin down, because there's a real distinction — and one thing I said earlier that needs correcting.

**The heuristic is code, not data.** `CenterlineFollowerHeuristic` ([heuristic_controller.py](training%20_scripts/util/heuristic_controller.py)) is a hand-written scripted controller that runs *live*, computing an action every step from the current sim state: it projects the wire tip onto the planned centerline, measures heading error and cross-track error, and commands translation/rotation to follow the path (retract-to-align phase, advance phase with near/inside-daughter regimes, plus an off-path pull-back behavior). No learning, no stored data — just a P-controller someone wrote. Historically it was used for demo harvesting and heuristic-seeding scripts, never during RL training.

**seed.npz is data** — 282,310 recorded transitions from the old harvest. And no — **P2 does not use seed.npz at all.** It can't: the new run's observations are 125-dim (the old file is 121) and, more fundamentally, actions now *mean* something different (a stored action from the old runs was the full command; in P2 the policy's action is a correction). The P2 launcher has no `--heatup_cache_file`. Instead the buffer fills from a fresh 20k-step heatup where every step is heuristic action + small random noise — live interaction, not the file.

So in P2, every single step of training and eval runs: **heuristic computes its action → policy adds a residual → sum (clipped) goes to the sim.**

**Now the correction.** Earlier I told you "the heuristic is what harvested the seed at 37.5% success" — that was wrong. The seed came from the *random-action heatup harvest* (`rcca_proc_heatup`), curated afterward; the 37.5% success rate describes the curated file's composition, not the heuristic's skill. Which means the heuristic's actual success rate on procedural RCCA is **unmeasured** — and code comments from its tuning era are not encouraging (the run-14 config note says it "produced our only success"). That's exactly what the baseline eval in this run exists to answer: with pretrain 0 and residual mean ≈ 0 at init, the first eval measures the pure heuristic, H₀. Let me check whether it's in yet:

Heatup just started (the ±9 mm/s / ±0.45 rad/s band confirms the 0.3-scale residual noise around the heuristic). It runs ~12 minutes, then the baseline eval — so **H₀ lands in roughly half an hour**, and the monitoring pass at :41 will record it.

To summarize the corrected picture:

| | What it is | Used in P2? |
|---|---|---|
| **Heuristic** | Scripted centerline-following controller, computes actions live every step | Yes — the base of every action, train and eval |
| **seed.npz** | Static file of old random-harvest transitions | No — obs- and action-space incompatible; fresh heatup instead |

And the honest stake this puts on the baseline eval: if H₀ comes back decent (anywhere near v2's early evals), the run genuinely starts at competence and RL only has to learn corrections. If H₀ comes back near zero — which the heuristic's tuning-era comments make a live possibility — then the "starts at heuristic competence" premise is falsified in the first hour rather than after days, and the sensible responses are either repairing the heuristic itself (it's just gains and thresholds) or accepting that the residual has to carry more of the load. Either way we'll know from the very first eval line, which is precisely why the baseline gate is built into the launcher.

## ▸ User [128]

does this student teacher method needs a heuristic

### Claude [128]

No — teacher-student itself doesn't need a heuristic. They're two independent ideas that P2a deliberately bundles, and it's worth separating them:

**Teacher-student (the privileged-learning part).** The core method is: train a *teacher* policy that gets to see privileged information (the 24-dim sim-side tail — true velocities, contact state, ground-truth branch — that a real deployment can't observe), then distill it into a *student* that acts from deployable observations only. Nothing about that requires a scripted controller. In the literature the teacher is usually trained by plain RL from scratch — but in domains with cheap simulation (locomotion runs billions of steps on massively parallel sims). Privileged obs make learning *easier* — cleaner state, sharper credit assignment — but they don't manufacture the initial successes that off-policy RL needs to get moving.

**The heuristic (the bootstrap part).** That's what solves the problem P1 just demonstrated: at our 7.5 Hz FEM throughput, from-scratch SAC produced essentially zero successes in 580k steps, and no amount of state observability fixes an empty success signal. A privileged-actor teacher trained from scratch would very likely have died the same death as RLPD — better inputs, same silence from the reward. The heuristic gives the run a behavior floor on day one, so RL's job shrinks from "discover siphon navigation" to "correct the controller where it fails."

So the bundle is: **heuristic = floor, privileged actor = learning capacity on top of the floor, distillation = deployability at the end.** Each addresses a different failure mode we've actually observed (P1's cold start, Gen-4's critic-only privileged info not reaching the policy, and the eventual sim-to-deployment gap).

Two follow-on points worth knowing:

- **The student won't need the heuristic bolted on.** In P2b we distill the teacher's *total* behavior (heuristic + residual), so the student ends up a standalone policy. The 4-dim heuristic-intent feature sits in the deployable prefix and only needs the planned centerline + tip tracking — available at deployment — so the student can keep it as an input or we drop it during distillation.
- **If H₀ comes back poor, the teacher-student plan survives.** The privileged-actor machinery is unchanged; we'd just need a different competence floor — repair the heuristic's gains (it's a small P-controller), or lean on the residual with the baseline as a weak prior rather than a strong one. The heuristic is the scaffolding, not the method.

The apparent direction inversion needs one verification (whether `trainer.state_dicts_network(x)` is a push or a fill-in-place request) before I flip it.

Next actions, in sequence: verify the call semantics in `singelagentprocess.py`, fix the sync direction, then R2 (the deadline guard — gate it on update-counter stall instead of wall-clock), the two invariant alarms, the in-container smoke gate proving a worker's weights change after one update cycle, and the `v1b` relaunch. I'll report when the smoke gate passes and the relaunch is up.

## ▸ User [142]

how did this bug got introduced ?

### Claude [142]

The best-supported reconstruction — two layers, one old and one mine:

**The latent layer (old):** `_update_algo_state_dicts` and the restart paths treat the main-process `self.algo` as the authoritative copy — networks are *pushed* algo→trainer, and only optimizer/scheduler state comes back. That asymmetry almost certainly dates from when training ran in the main process itself, where `self.algo` *was* always current and pushing it into a freshly spawned trainer was correct. When the trainer became a subprocess, the reconciliation kept that shape — correct at first spawn, wrong as a steady-state sync. It stayed harmless as long as whatever periodic trainer→algo pull exists on the healthy path kept running — v2 and P1 demonstrably learned (v2's 49%, P1's evolving snapshot md5s), so the normal cycle path did sync.

**The fatal layer (mine, e3bf215):** the `_restart_trainer` guard I added after the v2 deadlock re-seeds a fresh trainer from `self.algo`'s networks — lines 812/888. That's exactly the latent wrong-direction path. In this run, the 1800s trainer-result deadline was *shorter than the ~40-minute explore cycles* (P2's episodes run long — successes go deep, failures hit the 600-step cap), so the guard declared a healthy trainer hung every single cycle: kill trainer → respawn from `self.algo` = init → train 23k updates → kill again before any sync-back could land. Thirty-two times. The guard built to prevent silent death became a silent reset loop — and earlier runs never triggered it because their cycles fit inside 1800s.

So: an old asymmetry that was safe under its original assumptions, plus my recovery mechanism that violated those assumptions, plus this run's longer cycles as the trigger. Classic latent-bug-meets-new-code. Two caveats pending verification in the fix work: git blame to confirm the helper's age, and whether the healthy path's trainer→algo pull sits at cycle end or eval boundary (that determines whether *any* trained weights could have leaked through between restarts — the identical hashes say no, which is consistent with restart-every-cycle). The fix inverts the authority — trainer is truth, algo is the mirror — plus the R2 deadline gate on update-counter stall rather than wall-clock, and the hash-change alarm so this class of bug can never run silent for 24 hours again.

## ▸ User [144]

why were 2 model hypothesis rejected

### Claude [144]

Rejected on dominance, not on principle — every problem the two-actor design solves is solved cheaper by something else in the ladder, and the failure it targets hasn't even been demonstrated yet:

1. **The hypothesis it fixes is untested.** "A unimodal policy can't encode both modes" was never actually observed — no trained policy was ever deployed (the sync bug). What IS confirmed is the bimodal *target* (free-mode optimum ~25–30 mm/s, crunch ~0). Whether a single conditioned network fails to represent that is an open question v1b will answer first. Buying the most expensive fix before the failure is demonstrated is backwards.

2. **Mode-conditioning dominates it representationally.** Since the planned path lets us *compute* the mode, option A just puts the mode flag (junction proximity, crunch state, wrong-branch bits) into the observation. A single network conditioned on an explicit mode bit can realize two arbitrarily different behaviors — that's what conditioning does. Two separate actors only add value if conditioning provably saturates.

3. **If action *multimodality at one state* is the real issue, GMM wins.** The commit-vs-retract ambiguity lives at single states (junction: push or pull?), where the fix is a multimodal action head (GMM/QC-FQL, roadmap P3) — one net, one buffer, standard machinery. MoE with a hard gate still gives you one unimodal Gaussian per state unless the gate is perfect exactly where it's hardest (the boundary).

4. **Implementation risk in exactly the machinery that just burned us.** Two actors + gated buffers means surgery across `agent.py`'s single-policy assumption, worker weight-sync, checkpointing, eval, PER — the same plumbing where a one-line getter-return bug silently cost 24 hours. Split buffers also halve each actor's data and create boundary credit-assignment problems (who owns the transition step into the crunch?).

So the ladder is: v1b (does a plain conditioned policy compound at all?) → A (mode observation, ~6 dims, near-free) → C (GMM head) if the retract-probe stays flat — with B held as the falsifiable last resort if conditioning *and* multimodal heads both saturate. Your mode insight is fully adopted; it just enters through the observation and the action head before it justifies two networks.

## ▸ User [146]

what's the point of heatup

### Claude [146]

Heatup fills the empty replay buffer before any gradient update happens. Off-policy SAC learns by sampling past transitions — at launch the buffer has zero, and updates can't begin on nothing. So the run spends 20k steps just *collecting*.

In this residual design it does more than fill space:

1. **The data is already good.** Because the env composes heuristic + noise even for random actions, heatup collects ~heuristic-quality trajectories (~54% success in v1's heatup) rather than random flailing. The critic's very first batches contain deep RCCA threading, junction encounters, buckling, and successes — the states that matter.
2. **The ±30% noise band is the diversity engine.** Pure heuristic gives correlated, identical failures (your lack-of-diversity point); the noise decorrelates them, so the buffer contains *variations* around the script — including accidental retractions at stuck states, which is the raw material for learning recovery.
3. **It can't be replaced by the old seed file** — seed.npz is 121-dim obs with raw actions; this run is 125-dim with residual actions. Incompatible, so fresh collection is the only source.
4. **It's cheap here**: 20k steps ≈ 12 minutes across 16 workers, versus the 10k-update pretrain phase of the AWAC era which this design deliberately dropped (nothing to pretrain toward — the heuristic already provides the starting competence that pretrain used to buy).

Then the H₀ eval runs on the still-untrained policy (measuring the pure script as the control), and only when explore begins do updates start consuming the heatup data. It's the same role heatup always had — bootstrap the buffer — but the residual composition upgrades it from "random-walk filler" to "a pre-stocked library of near-competent behavior with useful mistakes."

**Root cause: the eval env doesn't fully reset device state between episodes.** `rot_inst` (and related wire state) carries over, so each worker's eval episodes follow a deterministic *orbit* — outcome is determined by episode **position in the sequence**, not by the seed. v1 and v1b landed in opposite orbit phases (at position 2, v1b sent 16/16 into RVA where v1 succeeded 13/16 — that alone is the entire 9-episode gap). **What this means:**
- **v1b stays up — do not restart.** Orbit phase is stable within a launch (v1's six windows repeated exactly), so the within-run control logic holds: v1b is judged by its delta from *its own* 36.7% baseline.
- **Cross-run absolute comparisons are suspended** — both 36.7% and 46.9% partly measure orbit phase, not skill. The honest cross-launch noise floor is ~±10 episodes, bimodal, not the ±1.8pp within-launch figure. "Beat v2's 49%" and the paper's eval-protocol section need this correction — within-run deltas only, until fixed.
- v1's celebrated "85/98 seeds deterministic" measured *position*-determinism, not seed-determinism.

**Queued actions:** P0 — hard-reset device state per eval episode (env fix, next relaunch); seed launches and dump `policy_0.pt` for reproducibility; use `episode_summary.jsonl` for eval accounting (worker logs drop each worker's final episode). Meanwhile v1b's real experiment proceeds: NET_SYNC gate, then whether learning lifts it above its own 36.7% floor — which, with the orbit now understood, is a cleaner question than the one we thought we were asking.

### Claude [148]

You're right, and for a reason that goes one level deeper than the doc's framing.

**Your core point stands:** H₀ has zero influence on training — it's a passive measurement; the gradients come from explore data. And since the *same* heuristic scores anywhere from 37% to 47% depending purely on orbit phase, v1b's 36.7% is not "the heuristic's ability" — it's one unlucky draw from the heuristic's band. A trained policy reaching 44% hasn't beaten the heuristic; it's landed inside what the script already does under a luckier phase. So the honest bar for "learned something beyond the script" is the **top of the heuristic's band, ~46–47%, plus margin** — not the local baseline.

**The deeper wrinkle that makes your bar not just preferable but necessary:** the within-run delta logic ("judge v1b against its own 36.7%") quietly assumes later evals replay the same orbit. But the orbit is *created by the policy's own actions* — the carried-over device state depends on what the previous episode did. The moment the policy differs from the heuristic, the orbit shifts, and eval-2's episode conditions are no longer H₀'s episode conditions. So within-run deltas are only clean while the policy is unchanged — precisely when they're uninteresting. Once learning starts, the only robust claim is against the phase-independent band.

**So the working criteria become:** any v1b eval **≥ ~49–50%** (band top + ~2σ within-launch noise) = genuine learning beyond the heuristic; anything in 37–47% = ambiguous, could be orbit reshuffling; and the **P0 eval-state reset gets promoted from "next relaunch nicety" to the fix that makes the whole measurement meaningful** — it collapses the band back to a single H₀ and restores both cross-run comparability and clean per-seed attribution. I'd still let v1b run meanwhile — it costs nothing, the NET_SYNC gate and Q-health checks are about infrastructure not eval interpretation, and if it posts a 50%+ eval that's decisive under your bar regardless of orbit. But the moment we relaunch for any reason, the reset fix goes in first, and I'll write the ~49–50% criterion into the monitoring prompt now so every future pass judges against the band, not the phase draw.

### Claude [155]

They're two different networks — the confusion is that "actor" sounds like one fixed thing, but teacher and student are *both* actors, existing at different stages:

**Now (P2a, the run that's training):** there is one actor — the **teacher**. Input width 125, privileged tail included. It's learning by RL. It will never be deployed; its job is to become as good as possible with perfect perception, establishing the performance ceiling.

**Later (P2b):** we instantiate a **second, separate policy network** — the student. Its input layer is only the 101 deployable dims (tracking, target offset, last action, guidance, heuristic intent — all obtainable from fluoroscopy + the planned path), plus a short observation history. The tail physically doesn't fit into its input; there's nothing to leak. It is *not* trained by RL — it's trained by supervised imitation via DAgger: roll out episodes, and at each visited state ask the teacher (with its privileged view) "what action?", then regress the student to reproduce that action *from the deployable view alone*. The student drives, the teacher labels — so the student learns to act correctly in the states its own behavior visits, which is DAgger's fix for compounding drift.

**How the student can match behavior it "can't see":** most of the tail is *inferable* from the history of observables — contact and slack manifest as tracking-motion vs commanded-motion discrepancies over a few steps; velocities are finite differences of tracking. The teacher gets these truths for free; the student must reconstruct them from temporal patterns, which is exactly why the history goes in (and why ep_step goes out). Whatever genuinely cannot be reconstructed becomes the **teacher–student gap** — the honest, measurable price of deployability, reported as student-eval-with-no-tail vs teacher ceiling. Yesterday's saliency probe already tells us where that gap will concentrate: crunch-mode behaviors driven by the contact dims.

**The deployed artifact** is then: student policy + the scripted heuristic underneath it (which needs only the planned centerline and tip tracking — both clinically available) composing actions exactly as now. Nothing in the inference path touches simulator internals. So: the actor being trained today is the non-deployable teacher; the actor that ships is the student cloned from it — same role in the architecture, different eyes.

## ▸ User [159]

how are hard recoveries defined; recoveries meant went to target right?

### Claude [159]

Two separate things, and the second is an important clarification — **no, "recovery" does not mean it reached the target.**

**What "recovery" means in this tracker.** It's a *local* escape from a stall, not a successful episode. The detector fires a "stuck event" when the wire is being pushed (`cmd_action[0] > 2 mm/s`) but path progress (`proj_s`) stalls for ≥12 consecutive steps. A **recovery** = the wire then gets *past that stuck point* — progress exceeds where it had stalled (`proj_s > pre-stuck max + 1 mm`). That's it. The episode can recover from a stall mid-run and still fail later (run out of steps, get stuck again elsewhere). So recovery events and episode success are **different axes**:
- *Recovery* = a per-event, mid-episode escape from one stall.
- *Success* (the `succ%` column) = the whole episode reached target (terminated ∧ not truncated).

**The three recovery flavors** are graded by how much the guidewire was *pulled back* (retraction depth `r` = peak insertion at stall onset − deepest point during the stall, in mm) before it got past the stuck point:

| type | retraction before escaping | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **grind** | `r < 1 mm` | brute-forced through — barely pulled back, just kept pushing |
| **soft** | `1 ≤ r ≤ 8 mm` | the wanted move: ease slack a little, then re-advance |
| **hard** | `r > 8 mm` | escaped only after a big pullback |
| **unrecovered** | — | never got past the stuck point before the episode ended |

So **hard recovery = it did resume forward progress past the stall, but only after retracting more than 8 mm** — a clumsy, expensive escape (lose a lot of ground to get unstuck), versus soft's efficient small ease.

**Why this matters for reading the table.** Because recovery is local, the counts can't be summed into "good outcomes." An episode with a hard recovery early can still be an unrecovered failure at a later stall, or a timeout. And crucially, most *successes* have **zero** stuck events — they thread cleanly and never trigger the detector — which is exactly the evidence behind the correction I just gave you: the 36%→60% gain came from cleaner navigation (fewer stalls to begin with), while the soft-recovery skill on the stalls that do happen stayed flat. The recovery table describes behavior *at stalls*; the success column describes *whole episodes*; they only partially overlap.

One honest caveat on the thresholds: the 8 mm soft/hard cut and the 12-step stall window are my chosen definitions, not the environment's — they're calibrated to be reasonable but the absolute soft/hard split would shift if we moved them. That's why I've been reading *trends and comparisons across evals* rather than the raw numbers, and why the tracker prints its thresholds at the top so any relaunch stays comparable.

## ▸ User [161]

what's The P0 eval-state-reset fix?

### Claude [161]

Let me ground this in the actual code rather than describe it from the log-based diagnosis — I want to point you at the real mechanism and reset path:

Found the actual mechanism — and it's more specific than the log-based diagnosis said. Here's the real bug, at [sofabeamadapter.py:99](eve/eve/intervention/simulation/sofabeamadapter.py#L99):

```python
def reset_devices(self):
    x = self._instruments_combined.m_ircontroller.xtip.value
    self._instruments_combined.m_ircontroller.xtip.value = x * 0.0        # insertion → 0  ✓
    ri = self._instruments_combined.m_ircontroller.rotationInstrument.value
    ri = self._rng.random(ri.shape) * 2 * np.pi                           # rotation → RANDOM
    self._instruments_combined.m_ircontroller.rotationInstrument.value = ri
    ...
```

**What it does:** every episode reset zeros the wire's insertion (correct) but sets each device's initial **rotation** to a random value — and it draws that from `self._rng`, the simulation's RNG. Now trace the seeding: `intervention.reset(seed)` reseeds *its own* `self._np_random` ([monoplanestatic.py:145](eve/eve/intervention/monoplanestatic.py#L145)), but the call it makes to `simulation.reset(...)` passes **no seed**, so the simulation's `self._rng` is never reseeded per episode. It free-runs.

**Why that produces the orbit:** because `self._rng` advances but never resets, the starting twist of eval episode N is a function of *how many draws happened before it* — i.e., the episode's **position in the sequence**, not its seed. Same seed at position 2 vs position 40 → different starting rotation → different outcome. And a fresh launch seeds `_rng` from a different point in its construction history, so v1 and v1b's episode-2 got *different* rotation phases → 46.9% vs 36.7% for the identical untrained policy. That's the whole ±10-episode cross-launch swing, and it's why "85/98 deterministic seeds" was really measuring position-determinism.

**The fix (P0):** make the initial rotation a deterministic function of the *episode seed*, not RNG history. In `intervention.reset()`, when a seed is provided, reseed the simulation's RNG too (thread the seed into `simulation.reset` / stash it for `reset_devices`), so each eval seed always draws the same starting rotation regardless of position or launch. Training keeps its randomization (seeded by each episode's train seed — fine, diversity preserved); eval becomes fully reproducible and seed-determined, which collapses the orbit noise to zero and restores cross-run comparability.

**One honest caveat before I commit it:** this is a mechanism I just located that *exactly* explains position-dependent, launch-varying evals — stronger than the deep-dive's vaguer "rot_inst carries over" — but I'd verify with a cheap test first: two short eval passes with the same seed should currently produce *different* rotations (bug present) and *identical* ones after the fix. There's also a SOFA-ordering subtlety (the `Simulation.reset(root)` call right after could interact with the rotation set), which the same-seed test would flush out.

Want me to run that reproducibility test and, if it confirms, build the fix? It's independent of the running v1b container (a code change to the eval reset path, deployed only on the next relaunch), so it won't disturb the run in progress.

### Claude [164]

Good catch — you did raise it, and I fragmented it across that list instead of presenting it as the coherent "two-mode" family you're thinking of. Let me lay it out properly, because it actually splits along **two axes**, and a robust stuck strategy needs both.

**Axis 1 — the model can *represent* two modes (architecture).** This is where your "two actors for two classified modes" proposal sits, and it's a spectrum from cheap to heavy:

| option | what it is | status in my list |
|---|---|---|
| **Mode-conditioning via observation** | one policy, but fed a path-derived mode signal (wrong-branch flag, stuck-duration EMA, arclength-to-junction) so it can behave differently in each mode | I buried this in #5 (path-context obs) — it *is* your "encode the modes via planned path" idea, the cheapest form |
| **Multimodal action head (GMM)** | one net, but outputs a mixture so it can hold commit-vs-retract at a single state instead of averaging them | #15, "backup" |
| **Two-actor + dual mode-classified buffers** | your explicit proposal — separate actors for stuck/non-stuck, path-classified, each with its own buffer, trained in one run | I marked this **"rejected"** — and that was too strong |

**Axis 2 — the stuck mode gets *trained densely* (data/curriculum).** This is the "more robust stuck strategy" half, and it's independent of architecture:

| option | what it is | status |
|---|---|---|
| **Stuck-lane sampling (E3)** | a dedicated sampling stream that oversamples stuck-state transitions every batch | **already built** in the codebase (env5 flat-index 89/103), used on machine-2's v3a plan; never run on the P2 line |
| **Stuck-restore curriculum (E4/D)** | *start* episodes from harvested stuck states, so recovery becomes the on-policy path to reward instead of a rare accident | #6, parked (blocked on machine-2 pool) |

**On the reconsideration you're prompting:** I rejected the two-actor MoE as a *first* move, and I stand by that ordering — mode-conditioning (Axis-1 row 1) dominates it representationally (a single net conditioned on an explicit mode bit can already realize two different behaviors), and if the failure is single-state multimodality, GMM is cleaner than a hard gate that's weakest exactly at the mode boundary. But "rejected forever" was wrong — the honest status is **deferred last-resort**: if a well-conditioned single policy *and* a GMM head both fail to hold the two regimes, the two-actor dual-buffer is the fallback. It should be on the parked list as that, not struck off.

So the corrected framing of the whole family: **combine one Axis-1 lever with one Axis-2 lever.** The cheapest robust-stuck bundle is *mode observation (#5) + stuck-restore (#6)* — give the policy the "you're off-plan / stuck" signal *and* dense practice at those states — which is exactly the v2 bundle. If that plateaus, escalate the architecture (GMM), and two-actor is the last rung.

Want me to write this two-axis framing into `RL_IMPROV_18_P2_DESIGN.md` as an explicit "stuck-mode strategy ladder," and re-file the two-actor MoE from "rejected" to "deferred last-resort" so it stops falling off the list?

## ▸ User [166]

we are not restoring anything ; right ? hwo are you going to get the crunch steps ; are you going to get it while training tr will you get it from the last run

### Claude [166]

Right — **no restoring in the lane design.** Let me separate the three things cleanly, because the doc bundled them:

**1. The crunchpass lane needs no restore at all.** It's purely a replay-sampling change. Episodes flow in exactly as they always have (normal resets from the insertion point, normal exploration); the only change is at `push()`: for each step we compute `crunch_sig(obs)` — the 5-feature rule — AND it with "did this episode succeed" (known at push, since push receives the whole episode), and set a flag. Sampling then draws a fixed batch fraction from flagged transitions via the existing third-lane SumTree. No checkpoint saving, no episode restarts from saved states. The crunch-entry *restore* idea is a separate, optional, later lever (and blocked on machine-2 re-harvesting anyway) — it's not part of the minimal bundle.

**2. Where the crunch steps come from: live, during the new training run.** The lane fills itself continuously — every success the run collects contributes its crunch-passage steps as it's pushed. And because a residual run starts at heuristic competence (~40–50% success from heatup onward), productive-crunch transitions exist *from the first heatup episodes* — no cold-start for the lane. The only thing taken **from the last run** is the classifier's *weights*: fit offline once on v1b's retained chunks (already prototyped, AUC ~0.94), then hardcoded — at training time it's just a dot product on 5 obs features, no learning, no extra compute.

**3. The last run's data *could* optionally pre-seed the lane — but there's a fork.** v1b's chunks (especially the crunch-rich eval3 era) are action-compatible (same residual-on-same-heuristic) and could be pushed at launch as a pool-2 cache. But this only works **if the obs layout stays 125** — the moment we add the path-context observation dims (the A lever, 125→~131), every stored v1b transition becomes obs-incompatible and we start fresh. So the choice is:

- **v1c-minimal**: crunchpass lane only, obs unchanged → *can* seed pool-2 from v1b's eval3-era chunks + keeps all v1b comparability. Cheapest, purest test of your two-pool idea.
- **v2-full**: lane + path-context obs → fresh data only (lane still self-fills fine), but adds the wrong-branch signal that targets the other failure channel.

My lean: **v1c-minimal first** — one variable (the lane), seedable, directly tests whether success-conditioned crunch resampling moves the ~62% plateau, with the obs change held back as the next lever. But it's your call which fork to build.

## ▸ User [167]

hwo will you alternate teh two modes ; equally ?

### Claude [167]

Not equally — mixed *within* every batch at a fixed minority fraction, and 50/50 would be a mistake for this pool. The reasoning:

**Mechanism: within-batch mixing, not alternation.** Same as the existing lanes — every batch of 256 draws, say, ~20% from the crunchpass lane's SumTree and the rest from the general buffer. Every gradient step sees both modes in one batch, so there's no objective ping-ponging between updates (alternating whole batches *would* oscillate the policy between two objectives — the thing we don't want).

**Why the crunch fraction should be ~0.15–0.25, not 0.5:**

1. **Pool size reality.** Crunch-signature steps are ~14–22% of transitions, and after success-conditioning pool-2 is maybe **3–8% of the buffer**. Sampling it at 50% of every batch over-weights it ~10×, and the gradient becomes dominated by a narrow state distribution — the effective-batch-collapse problem (same failure family as E1b's weight-concentration concern), plus general navigation competence — the thing that actually got us to 62% — starts eroding from neglect.
2. **The mode imbalance is the point, but bounded.** Natural frequency under-trains crunch (that's the whole motivation); a 0.2 fraction already over-samples pool-2 by ~3–5× its natural rate, which is a strong tilt without drowning the rest.
3. **Precedent in this codebase**: clean lane ran at 0.3, the E3 stuck-lane design chose 0.15. And note the overlap — crunchpass transitions are by construction a *subset* of successful episodes, i.e. roughly a subset of the clean lane. So the sane composition is something like **0.2 clean + 0.2 crunchpass + 0.6 general** (crunchpass acting as a sharpened carve-out of what the clean lane was crudely amplifying), rather than stacking 0.3 + 0.5 on top.

**Tuned by evidence, not fixed forever:** start at 0.2, watch two dials — (a) crunch-passage escape/success rate rising (the lane doing its job), (b) general and clean success *not* sagging (the overdose alarm). If pool-2 grows large and healthy, the fraction can ramp; if general performance dips, back off. The launcher flag makes it a one-knob experiment.

And on the **conditioning axis** (mode bit / GMM), no alternation is needed at all: each sampled transition carries its own classifier bit, so both modes train simultaneously in whatever mixture the sampler delivers — the fraction above *is* the mode balance knob for learning.

### Claude [177]

Good catch — let me not hand-wave it, let me check the raw fields directly:

You've found a real data-integrity issue — and it's two things stacked. First the direct answer, then the deeper problem it exposed:

**`explore_step` is the global 16-worker cumulative counter, not steps-in-those-200-episodes.** All 16 workers step in parallel and share one counter, so between logged episode completions it advances by *all* workers' steps. That alone explains why the number is large — but it doesn't fully explain it, so I checked the raw fields, and found the actual problem:

**`episode_summary.jsonl` is missing ~60% of explore episodes.** The tell: summing every logged episode's `steps` field = 1.9M, but the counter reaches 3.52M explore steps. Since heatup (explore_step=0) and eval (frozen counter) don't advance it, the logged *explore* episodes account for only ~40% of the 3.52M explore steps. So each of my "200-episode" buckets actually spanned ~500 real episodes of exploration — the bucket labels were over *logged* episodes, a subsample.

**Why this matters and why it might not:**
- The **eval** blocks in this file are complete and correct (98 each; eval3 = 80/98 = 81.6%, exactly matching the Quality line). So everything I told you about the evals and the CCA/ICA/siphon split stands — that came from the complete eval records.
- The **explore** success rates (the 200-ep buckets, the ~62% plateau) came from the subsample. If the dropping is random, ~62% holds. If it's length-biased — short successes stream through while long 600-step failures get dropped under queue pressure — then **62% is biased high** and true explore success is lower. I can't rule that out from this file alone.

So the honest status: eval numbers solid, explore numbers provisional. Let me recompute explore success from the authoritative source — the worker logs' `EPISODE_OUTCOME` lines, which log *every* episode — as ground truth:

While that runs — a monitoring event just landed that matters: **v1bp's H₀ baseline = 45.9%**, which is squarely inside v1b's 37–47% band. That's the port-integrity gate **passing** — the reward-pair changes didn't leak into dynamics; the reward-blind heuristic scores exactly where it should. (More on v1bp when it hits eval1.)

Let me get the ground-truth explore number:

Ground truth is in, and it vindicates your catch while — reassuringly — leaving the *conclusions* intact. Here's the reconciliation:

| source | explore episodes | success% |
|---|---|---|
| `episode_summary.jsonl` (what I bucketed) | ~5,200 logged | 61.5% |
| worker logs `EPISODE_OUTCOME` (every episode) | **14,433** | 64.3%* |

*\*includes ~10% eval contamination — my wall-time eval filter matched nothing (guessed timestamps wrong), so true explore-only is ~62–63%.*

**What you caught (real):** `episode_summary.jsonl` logs only ~36% of explore episodes — 14.4k actually ran, ~5.2k were logged — while the `explore_step` column is the global 16-worker counter. So my "200 episodes per bucket" was 200 *log-lines*, each bucket actually spanning ~550 real episodes, and the step numbers are cumulative-global. The bucket labels were wrong on both axes. Fair catch — that file is a lossy stream, not a complete ledger.

**What survives (the part that matters):** the success *rate* is robust. Ground truth ~62–63% vs the subsample's 61.5% — within ~1–2 points — so the subsampling was essentially unbiased w.r.t. outcome (not the length-bias I worried could inflate it). So every rate-based conclusion stands: the ~62% explore plateau, the flat 55–68% band, the eval3-era being ~63%, and therefore the 81.6% eval sitting cleanly above concurrent explore. And the CCA/ICA/siphon split was from the complete eval records, untouched by any of this.

**What I'll fix going forward:** treat `episode_summary.jsonl` as rate-only, never as an episode ledger or a step ruler — use worker-log `EPISODE_OUTCOME` counts (complete) or `explore_step` ranges for anything involving counts or timing. And I owe you a correction to my own earlier "200-ep bucket" framing: those were fine as success rates, wrong as episode/step counts.

Net: the anomaly was a logging artifact, not a problem with the findings — but it was a genuine hole in how I was reading and labeling the data, and it took your eye to surface it.

- Hashing `pathfinder.path_points_vessel_cs` is useless as an anatomy check — the planned path moves with the target, so it differs across seeds even in an identical tree (my first preflight "passed" both ways and was meaningless).

| landmark | cum. len | diam |

| supraclinoid (C6) | ~255 mm | 3.5 |
| **terminus (C7, MCA/ACA bif)** | **~265 mm** | 3.2 |

The vessel is one branch, `"rcca"`, ending **at** the MCA/ACA bifurcation. M1 is the MCA's first segment, which starts at that bifurcation and runs laterally — so yes, it lies beyond the siphon, and beyond everything we navigate. Our deepest targets sit at or just before the terminus.

**What that means for my depth bins** (they're anatomically defensible, but should be relabelled precisely):
- **"CCA" (<146 mm)** — CCA + proximal cervical ICA
- **"ICA-mid" (146–210 mm)** — distal C1 + petrous genu C2
- **"siphon" (≥210 mm)** — the true siphon: cavernous C4 (both genua) + supraclinoid C6, up to the C7 terminus

**What nothing achieves:** the siphon, 0/30 for every model tested. That's not a tuning problem; it's a capability boundary sitting exactly at the ~180° cavernous genua the vessel definition itself flags as the overshoot region.

**Three corrections the paper now needs:**
1. The headline number is **35.7% on real anatomy**, not 81.6% — and 81.6% was one lucky *generated* variant, not even a real vessel.
2. The reward pair, our most recent multi-day experiment, is a **null result** on both honest protocols. Worth reporting as such rather than quietly dropping.
3. The procedural generator produces **easier** vessels than the real one (57.1% vs 35.7%), so "trained on procedurally varied anatomies" doesn't imply robustness to real ones — the distribution gap runs the wrong way.

Both re-extractions running with the exact filter. To answer your question directly on coverage — **yes, all four kinds are tracked everywhere**, and here's the reasoning behind each distinction, which is what determines whether these tables mean anything:

**Why a stall is defined as "pushing but not progressing"** — not simply "not progressing." A wire that's deliberately retracting or rotating isn't stuck; it's manoeuvring. Requiring `cmd_action[gw_trans] > push_min` while `proj_s` fails to advance isolates the case where the policy *is trying to go forward and the vessel won't let it*. The counter decays by 2 rather than resetting to 0, so a single noisy command sign-flip inside a genuinely stuck push doesn't erase the evidence.

**Why classify by retraction depth** — because escaping a stall is not one behavior, it's three with very different clinical meaning:
- **grind** (<1 mm): the wire never backed off; it forced through. This is the heuristic's native move and the one that caps performance — it works in wide vessels and fails at the genua.
- **soft** (1–8 mm): back off just enough to unload the stored slack, re-orient, advance. This is the behavior a human operator uses and the one we've been trying to induce.
- **hard** (>8 mm): escaped, but gave up a lot of ground — costly, and usually a sign the wire had already coiled.
- **unrecovered**: the stall was terminal for that episode.

**Why measure retraction from actual insertion, not commanded action** — a retract command that moves nothing (wire wedged) would otherwise be scored as a soft recovery. Using `peak_insertion − deepest_insertion` during the stall counts only length that actually came out.

**Why the three-way success split matters** — an episode can succeed *because* it recovered, or succeed *having never stalled at all*. Those attribute to completely different skills, and lumping them is exactly how I earlier mistook "success ≈ recovery" for a real relationship. T2 separates them and reports what fraction of all successes actually flowed through the recovery channel; T3 then asks whether soft recovery converts to episode success better than grinding — the hypothesis the whole crunchpass/two-mode design rests on.

The decisive column is the last one. In v1b, recovery's contribution to overall success **collapses from 29% to 6%**. Early on, roughly a third of all wins were rescues; by the end, almost every win is an episode that simply never jammed. Combined with T1, this is the whole story of the run: the policy migrated from "get stuck, fight out" to "don't get stuck", and that migration *is* the performance gain.

An episode that pushes 600 steps without ever jamming has by construction arrived; one ending jammed by construction hasn't. ## T3 — Does recovery *type* predict episode success?

**v1b**

| recovery profile | episodes | episode succ% | median steps | mean retract mm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| soft (any) | 820 | 95% | 187 | 4.9 |
| hard (no soft) | 248 | 92% | 227 | 13.7 |
| **grind only** | 362 | **99%** | **107** | 0.1 |
| unrecovered (any) | 6065 | 1% | 600 | 13.5 |
| never stalled | 7196 | 100% | 41 | 0.0 |

**v1bp**

| recovery profile | episodes | episode succ% | median steps | mean retract mm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| soft (any) | 714 | 76% | 296 | 6.2 |
| hard (no soft) | 195 | 65% | 370 | 15.2 |
| **grind only** | 159 | **95%** | **121** | 0.1 |
| unrecovered (any) | 3584 | 1% | 600 | 11.0 |
| never stalled | 3388 | 100% | 43 | 0.0 |

**What this shows.** This tests the assumption the entire two-mode/crunchpass design rests on: that **soft** recovery — the retract-and-re-advance move — is the valuable skill.

It isn't, at least not as measured. **Grind-only episodes outperform soft in both runs** — 99% vs 95% in v1b, 95% vs 76% in v1bp — and do it in roughly a third of the steps. Hard recovery is worst of all.

I'd read this as a **confound rather than a refutation of retraction per se**: recovery type is largely a proxy for *stall severity*, not policy skill. A jam you can grind through was mild; one that forces an 8 mm withdrawal was severe, and severe jams live in the deeper, tighter anatomy where the episode was likely doomed anyway. So conditioning on recovery type is partly conditioning on difficulty. Either way, the practical conclusion stands: **you cannot justify amplifying soft recoveries on this evidence**, and the crunchpass lane's premise needs the confound broken first (compare soft vs grind *within* matched depth strata).

## T5 — Head-to-head, whole run

| metric | v1b | v1bp | reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| episodes / explore steps | 14,691 / 4.06M | 8,040 / 2.55M | |
| **episode succ%** | **58.6** | 52.8 | v1b ahead (57.4% at matched 2.55M) |
| stalled-ep% | 51.0 | 57.9 | v1bp jams **more** |
| events | 13,013 | 10,999 | |
| **recovery succ%** | 53.4 | **67.4** | v1bp escapes **far better** |
| soft% | 22.6 | 29.5 | |
| hard% | 10.9 | 17.3 | |
| grind% | 19.8 | 20.6 | equal |
| **unrec%** | 46.6 | **32.6** | v1bp leaves far fewer terminal jams |
| **recovered-ep succ%** | **95.2** | 77.0 | v1bp's escapes **convert worse** |
| % successes via recovery | 15.8 | 19.4 | |
| **mean cath-lead frac** | 0.34 | **0.04** | the catheter shove is gone |

**What this shows.** The reward-pair verdict, and it's a genuinely instructive split result.

**The pair did exactly what it was designed to do.** Catheter-lead — the shove pathology it targeted — fell from 0.34 to **0.04**. Escape rate rose 53 → 67%, terminal jams fell 47 → 33%, soft share rose. It even abolished the recovery decay (see T1/T6).

**And it gained nothing.** Episode success is *lower* (52.8 vs 58.6; 57.4 at matched budget). The mechanism: v1bp's careful, non-shoving gait jams more often (57.9%), and its recoveries convert to episode success at only 77% versus 95% — because they're slow. From T3, its soft recoveries take 296 median steps against a 600 cap; a recovery that eats half the budget often can't finish the journey.

This is the cleanest evidence in the program that **you can move an internal behaviour decisively and still gain nothing on the outcome** — worth reporting as a result in its own right.

|---|---|---|
| **v1b** | **r = −0.82** | r = −0.76 |

**What this shows.** A direct test of the intuition that success tracks recovery. In v1b it's **strongly negative** — periods of better recovery are periods of *worse* success, because both are downstream of how often the wire is jamming at all. My earlier "success% ≈ recovery%" reading was wrong; it came from comparing a per-event rate against a per-episode rate without noticing they're different units.

v1bp's near-zero correlation is itself informative: the reward pair decoupled the two, which is what preserving the recovery skill looks like statistically.

## 2. What kills v1bp's recovered-but-failed episodes: **the clock**

Of v1bp's 246 recovered-but-failed episodes: **91% died at the 600-step cap** (`reason=max_steps`), median **61 mm short of target**, last recovery at **97% of the episode** (still fighting stalls at the buzzer), median **3 stall events** vs 2 for recovered-successes. They escaped every jam and simply ran out of time mid-journey — serial re-stalling plus slow escapes exhaust the budget. (Ending *stuck* is excluded by construction — that would classify as unrecovered.)

| band | v1b rec-ep succ% | v1bp rec-ep succ% |
|---|---|---|

Bins 3–5 (the turbulence phase around the 40% dip) recovered deep stalls but converted almost none of them; by bins 6–7 v1bp converts recovered episodes at 94–95% — **it eventually learned to make recoveries pay**. | eval run | fails | still **advancing** at cap | **jammed** at cap | med d_tgt (jammed) |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Three decisive facts:

1. **In v1b's 1000-step rerun, zero successes took more than 600 steps.** Every episode that succeeded did so within the old budget; the extra 400 steps converted nothing. (Two seeds that "flipped" between runs succeeded in *under* 600 steps the second time — that's SOFA run-to-run stochasticity, not clock rescue.)

2. **v1bp's eval failures are jammed, not slow.** Only 3 of 54 failures on the 50-anatomy eval were still advancing when time ran out (upper bound ≈ +3 pp even if all three converted), and **0 of 69** on real patient. The rest sat at a stall frontier ~44–49 mm from target with no forward motion in the last 100 steps.

3. The classifier itself calibrates against ground truth poorly in the optimistic direction: of the 3–4 v1b failures flagged "advancing at cap" at 600, essentially none actually succeeded when given 1000. Even the moving ones just meet their next stall.

**Why this doesn't contradict the explore finding:** the 91%-die-at-cap result was for *explore* episodes under σ-noise — a wiggling, slow gait that genuinely runs out of clock while en route. Eval runs the deterministic mean policy, which fails differently: it drives to a hard stall and grinds there forever. Same policy, two failure modes — the clock kills the noisy gait, the wall kills the deterministic one. (Also worth noting: v1bp's real-patient failure profile is statistically identical to v1b's — consistent with our earlier finding that they solve the identical 35 seeds.)

So a 1000-step v1bp eval isn't worth the compute: expected gain ~0–3 pp on generated anatomies, ~0 on real patient. The binding constraint at eval time is the siphon wall, not the step budget.

## The failure is a geometric arrest, not a policy failure

On the real patient, failures don't scatter — they stop at the same place:

| model | fail | failed arrest median | in [152.5, 154.5] | max solved path_len |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1b | 69 | **153.4 mm** | 63/69 = **91%** | **156.2** |
| v1bp | 69 | **153.3 mm** | 63/69 = **91%** | **156.2** |
| **H0 — hand-written heuristic** | 74 | **153.3 mm** | 41/74 = 55% | **156.2** |

**H0 is a centerline follower with no learned parameters.** A station that arrests it and two independently trained policies at the same tenth of a millimetre cannot be a policy defect — that's environment.

**And it isn't at the siphon.** 153.4 mm is 7 mm past the ICA-mid cut and **57 mm before the siphon band begins at 210 mm**. Our "siphon 0/30" headline is mislabelled: nothing ever reaches the siphon to fail there.

## It's not just the real patient — I checked, and it's worse than claimed

Pooled arrest on the 50 generated anatomies scatters (SD 34 mm), which looks like ordinary navigation failure. Grouping by anatomy hash shows why that was misleading — each anatomy has its *own* deterministic wall: **80% (v1b) / 69% (v1bp)** of anatomies with ≥2 deep failures have within-anatomy SD < 2 mm, carrying **45% / 41% of all failure mass**. The clincher is that the same anatomies wall at the same station for *both* models — 11d068 @152.1, bfadcd @166.3, 8ba8a3 @157.2, dd7d9c @160.8, all ±0.00.

## Where the workflow was wrong

It claimed a "clean cut" — max solved 156.2, min failed 164.2, so every real-patient failure is beyond-wall. **That's false.** Measured min failed `path_len` is **103.2 mm**. So ~6 of 69 failures are genuine shallow navigation failures. The wall dominates but doesn't explain everything, and there's real (small) RL headroom.

## What this costs us

Three prior conclusions have to be downgraded, and I'd rather say so plainly: the 50-anatomy eval measures the mesh as much as the policy; the reward-pair null and today's dither null are both re-explained (neither could move a geometric wall — they were good tests aimed at a bottleneck that wasn't there); and **my r = −0.82 avoidance-not-escape finding is now provisional**, because it pools walled and non-walled episodes, and a stall against a hard wall isn't the same event as a stall in navigable vessel. That re-stratification is pure CPU and worth doing before the reports get used further.

Two candidate mechanisms, both indefensible regardless of which is the wall: **9.94 mm straight collision chords** (`jshaped.py:50`, 0.1 edges/mm at `proximity=0.0`) inside a 1.2–2.5 mm lumen, and **25–43% lumen erosion** (`meshing.py:41-56`, anisotropic voxels + double `gaussian_smooth` + `decimate(0.99)`).

**The recommended next step is cheap and decisive:** an H0 arrest-station A/B — 2×2 over collision density × mesher, scored on *arrest station* rather than success%, since the station is deterministic to 0.1 mm while success% at n=30 has almost no power. ~4–6 GPU-hours, no training, invalidates no checkpoint. ## ▸ User [203]

Can you explain more; I didnt get

### Claude [203]

Let me build it up from scratch.

## The setup

Every episode, the wire travels along a planned centerline from the neck vessels up toward the brain. We measure progress as `proj_s` — **how many millimetres along that path the wire tip has reached.** The path looks like this:

```
0mm ────────── 146mm ──────────── 210mm ─────────── 265mm
    CCA (neck)  │   ICA-mid        │   SIPHON        │ end
                │                  │  (the tight     │
                │         ▲        │   S-curve)      │
                │      153.4mm     │                 │
                │    ← EVERYTHING STOPS HERE
```

An episode succeeds if the tip gets within 5 mm of its target. Different episodes get targets at different distances along that path.

## What I found in the logs

I parsed every real-patient episode and asked: *for the failures, how far did the wire actually get before it stopped?*

If failures were caused by bad policy decisions, those numbers should be **scattered** — one wire wanders off at 90 mm, another buckles at 170 mm, another times out at 200 mm. Instead:

| model | how far the failures got |
|---|---|
| v1b | 91% stopped between 152.5 and 154.5 mm — **51 of them at exactly 153.4** |
| v1bp | 91% stopped in the same window — **61 at exactly 153.3** |
| **H0 (the hand-written heuristic)** | also stops at **153.3 / 153.4** |

## Why this is the smoking gun — three separate reasons

**1. H0 has no learned parameters.** It's a hundred lines of hand-written code that steers toward the centerline. It cannot "fail to learn" anything. If a hand-written follower and two independently trained neural networks all stop at the same tenth of a millimetre, the thing stopping them is not in the policy — it's in the world.

**2. The success cutoff lines up exactly.** For all three models, the deepest target ever solved sits at `path_len = 156.2 mm`. The wall is at 153.4, and success needs the tip within 5 mm. So `153.4 + 5 = 158.4` — every target up to ~158 is reachable, everything past it is not. **Max solved 156.2 is precisely what a hard wall at 153.4 predicts.** It isn't a gradual difficulty curve; it's a cliff.

**3. Same effect on generated anatomies, at anatomy-specific stations.** This one I nearly missed. Pooled across the 50 generated anatomies, the stopping points *look* scattered (SD 34 mm) — like ordinary navigation failure. But when I grouped by which anatomy each episode ran on, each anatomy turned out to have its **own** fixed wall:

| anatomy | where v1b stops | where v1bp stops |
|---|---|---|
| 11d068 | 152.1 | 152.1 |
| bfadcd | 166.3 | 166.3 |
| 8ba8a3 | 157.2 | 157.2 |
| dd7d9c | 160.8 | 160.8 |

Two different neural networks, trained separately, stopping at *identical* millimetre readings on each mesh. That's geometry, not behaviour. **About 40–45% of all our 50-anatomy failures are this.**

## Why "siphon 0/30" was the wrong label

Look at the diagram again. **153.4 mm is 57 mm short of where the siphon even begins.** We've been reporting "the model can't get through the carotid siphon" — but nothing was ever *reaching* the siphon. It stops in the mid-ICA, well before the hard anatomy starts. We diagnosed a difficult-curve problem in a place the wire never visits.

## What likely causes it — two suspects, both plain bugs

**Suspect 1 — the wire is made of 10 mm straight sticks (for collision).** SOFA models the guidewire's collision shape as a chain of straight segments. The config gives 0.1 segments per mm, so an 885 mm wire gets 89 segments — **each one a straight 9.94 mm chord.** Now imagine pushing a rigid 10 mm matchstick around a bend whose radius is 4 mm inside a 2 mm-wide tube. It jams — no matter how skilfully you push. The real wire bends smoothly; the simulated collision shape can't.

**Suspect 2 — the vessel got shrunk during mesh conversion.** The anatomy is voxelized at 0.6 mm, then `gaussian_smooth` runs **twice**, then 99% of triangles are removed. Smoothing a thin tube erodes it. Offline measurement gives an effective radius of 0.52–0.62 mm where the true vessel is 1.25–1.40 mm — **less than half.** The wire is 0.36 mm, so it goes from comfortable to barely-fitting.

Both would stop the wire at roughly the same place — wherever the vessel first gets narrow and curvy. That's why the arrest number alone can't tell us which one it is.

## What this costs us, honestly

Several months of work targeted a bottleneck that wasn't there. The reward pair, the dither test — both were well-designed experiments, and both now have an obvious explanation for why they did nothing: **no reward function and no exploration noise can move a wall.**

It also puts my own earlier finding on probation. The r = −0.82 "improvement is avoidance, not escape" result pools walled and non-walled episodes together — and a "stall" against an impassable geometric wall is simply not the same event as a stall in navigable vessel. That number has to be recomputed within the non-walled episodes before it can be trusted. Same for the reports I built today.

## The test that settles it

Run the **heuristic** (no training at all) on the real patient, 2×2: collision segments at 0.1 vs 0.5 per mm, crossed with the current vs a finer mesher. Score **where it stops**, not success rate.

The reason this is a good test: the stopping point is reproducible to 0.1 mm across hundreds of episodes, so a handful of runs gives a completely unambiguous answer — whereas success rate at n=30 is so noisy it can't resolve anything. About 4–6 GPU-hours, no training, nothing invalidated.

If the wall moves when you fix the collision segments, that's the bug. If it moves with the finer mesh, that's the bug. If neither moves it, both theories die and the next suspect is device stiffness (both devices are set 80× softer than eve's own validated values).

I haven't run it — it modifies environment config, so I wanted your go-ahead first.

## ▸ User [204]

I thought we are generating random anatomy every training run so how come 2 different runs have identical anamies

### Claude [204]

Sharp catch — and the answer matters for whether my verification is valid at all. Let me check it rather than assert it:

**All 50 identical, zero different.** And that's by design — but you've put your finger on exactly the right distinction, because **training and evaluation generate anatomies differently.**

## Training: random, always changing

During a training run, each of the 16 workers has its own anatomy stream that regenerates every N episodes. Across v1b's 4 million steps and v1bp's 2.5 million, they saw thousands of different vessel trees, and there's no reason for any of them to coincide. Your intuition is correct for training.

## Evaluation: deliberately frozen and reproducible

The numbers in the wall analysis don't come from training. They come from the standalone evaluator I wrote a few days ago, which seeds anatomy generation **deterministically**:

```python
def env_eval_factory(worker_id: int):
    return make_env(a, seed=a.seed_base + 10000 * (worker_id + 1),
                    change_every=change_every, mode="eval")
```

With `SEED_BASE=900000` fixed in the launcher, worker 1 always gets seed 910000, worker 2 always 920000, and so on. Same seeds → same generator state → **byte-identical vessel geometry every time it runs**, regardless of which checkpoint is being evaluated.

That was the whole point: **you cannot compare two models on different anatomies.** If v1b scored 57.1% on one random set and v1bp 55.1% on a different random set, the gap could be entirely down to one set being easier. Freezing the eval set makes it a paired comparison — same 50 vessels, same 98 targets, only the policy changes.

## And that's what makes the wall evidence work

The check above isn't just housekeeping — it's load-bearing for the finding. Because the meshes are byte-identical, when I say anatomy `11d068` arrests v1b at 152.1 mm and arrests v1bp at 152.1 mm, those are **two different neural networks on the exact same vessel, stopping at the same millimetre.** That comparison would be meaningless if the anatomies merely had the same label but different geometry.

Worth noting how I know they're truly identical rather than just similarly named: the `anatomy=` tag is an **MD5 of the actual vessel branch coordinates**, not a seed or a filename. I switched to hashing real geometry after discovering earlier that the obvious identifiers lie — `mesh_fingerprint` is built from a seed that gets reassigned, and the planned path moves when the target moves, so both would have "matched" meaninglessly. Hashing the branch coordinates is the only identifier that can't fool you. Matching hashes means the same vertices.

So: three separate models on one real-patient anatomy stopping at 153.4 mm, and two models on 50 shared generated anatomies each stopping at that anatomy's own fixed station. Both comparisons are valid precisely because the eval geometry is frozen — which is the thing your question was probing.

## Your historical result is real

`RL_IMPROV_10_CHANGES.md:800` — the pid19116 fixed-mesh policy: CCA 45/45 = 100%, cervical ICA 33/40 = 82.5%, **siphon 6/13 = 46.2%**. The wire traversed the siphon routinely. So "geometrically impossible" was wrong.

## What I got wrong: my evaluator was measuring the wrong surface

This is the part that matters. My `--real_patient_anatomy` mode zeroes all the perturbation amplitudes, which does reproduce the patient's **centerlines** exactly — I verified that at the time and it's true. But I missed what happens next. From the class's own docstring at [rccavariedfrommesh.py:10](eve/eve/intervention/vesseltree/rccavariedfrommesh.py#L10):

> *"the whole tree is **re-meshed from centerlines** (voxel → marching-cubes)"*

The historical run loaded the **original segmented patient surface** straight from disk. Mine takes the same centerlines and rebuilds a brand-new surface around them. Same skeleton, completely different vessel wall. **So "real patient 35.7%" was never measured on the patient's anatomy** — it was measured on a reconstruction. That's a flaw in the evaluator I wrote, and it invalidates that row of the results matrix.

## And the reconstruction is unusable distally

| quantity | measured |
|---|---|
| whole arterial tree | 1,871 points / **3,721 triangles** |
| triangle edge length | **median 6.46 mm**, p90 11.9, max 25.8 |
| distal vessel diameter (true) | **2.5–3.4 mm** |

**The triangles are two to four times bigger than the vessel they represent.** `generate_mesh` ends with `decimate(0.99)` — it throws away 99% of the surface. Distally that vessel isn't a tube any more; it's a crude polygon whose cross-section pinches to nothing between vertices. Of course the wire jams at a fixed station: it's hitting a facet edge, and the same facet is in the same place every episode, which is exactly the deterministic 153.4 mm signature.

## Two things I'd previously suggested are now dead

I want to flag these rather than quietly drop them, since I put them to you an hour ago:

**Lumen erosion is refuted** — I measured it directly. Distal mean shrink is **1%** (1.71 mm true vs 1.69 mm meshed), and **0 of 15** distal stations are too tight for the 0.36 mm wire. The workflow's claimed 25–43% doesn't reproduce. The deviations are large but *two-sided* (−56% to +28%), which is faceting noise, not systematic shrinkage.

**The collision-chord theory is largely eliminated too** — by your evidence, not mine. The historical run used the same devices and settings and got through the siphon. A 9.94 mm straight collision chord would have stopped it there as well.

## The corrected picture

Gen-4 introduced procedural anatomy so each worker could see a different vessel. To do that it had to generate meshes on the fly — and the generator's settings silently replaced a properly resolved clinical surface with one that has no meaningful distal geometry. That single change explains the whole pattern: fixed-mesh runs hit 86% with 46% siphon; every procedural run since plateaus near 57% with 0% siphon; 40–45% of generated anatomies have a fixed wall; and reward/algorithm interventions all came back null because none of them can move a triangle.

**The test is now much better targeted:** set `decimate_factor` from 0.99 to ~0.5 (and/or finer voxels), regenerate, and re-run the heuristic on the real-patient centerlines scoring the arrest station. If the wall moves or vanishes, that's it. Worth running alongside: evaluate directly on the original patient surface mesh to reproduce your 46.2% siphon number under the current harness — that would confirm the harness is sound and only the mesh was bad.

**The smoke test already answers your question: the wall was the mesh.** With the original surface, 4/4 succeeded and one of them was a **siphon target at path_len 261 mm** — territory where previously *nothing* got past 153.4 mm across 246 episodes and three controllers.

Two things worth knowing about how the fix landed, because the first attempt was wrong in an instructive way:

**Simply swapping to `DualDeviceNav` was not the fix.** That smoke test gave `path_len` 594–752 mm against ~103–156 mm for every prior run, with the wire crawling near the LCCA. `DualDeviceNav` starts the wire at the **femoral entry** and threads the entire arch, and samples targets from four branches with no minimum arclength. I'd have been testing a different task on a policy never trained for it — and it would have read as a catastrophic failure. This is exactly what the 4-episode smoke test is for; running 98 straight away would have produced a confidently wrong headline.

**The correct fix keeps everything and swaps only the collision surface.** The varied class keeps its insertion at the (11) bridge, RCCA-only targets, same devices and frames; only the mesh is replaced by `DualDeviceNav`'s `FromMesh` output — the original `.obj` already rotated into the branch frame, which is the right surface for these (byte-identical) centerlines. One variable.

There was also a real implementation wrinkle: `_generate()` nulls `_mesh_path` and `reset()` calls it, so the re-meshed surface came back on the first reset. Patching that required a class-level method rather than a closure or a locally-defined class — both fail to pickle to spawned workers.

**Where the content lives inside the scripts** — the prose isn't in a data file, it's inline:

- **Captions**: `WHAT IT SHOWS` / `INFERENCE` strings sit next to each page's plotting code. In `report_stuck.py` they're the `SH5/IN5`, `SH6/IN6`, `SH7/IN7`, `SH8/IN8`, `SH11/IN11` pairs; in `report_single.py` they're `s1/i1` … `s9/i9`, branched on `IS_B` so each run gets its own wording.
- **Findings and implications pages**: the `F = [...]` and `IMP = [...]` lists near the end. In `report_single.py` these are computed from that run's own numbers (f-strings pulling from `SU`, `RC`, `GS`, `T4`, `REC_S`, `CAPPCT`), so edits to thresholds flow through automatically rather than needing the text updated by hand.
- **Layout/styling**: `table()`, `caption()`, `newpage()` at the top, plus the colour constants `C_B` / `C_BP` / `C_MAIN`.

**Input data** comes from [monitoring/extract_stuck.py](monitoring/extract_stuck.py), which produced `saved/stuck_v1b.jsonl` and `saved/stuck_v1bp.jsonl` from the worker logs. The reports recompute every table from those records, so you only need to re-run extraction if the underlying logs change.

One thing to flag before you edit for the paper: **the reports predate today's mesh finding.** Their headline conclusions — particularly r = −0.82 avoidance-not-escape, and the depth table showing 90–97% siphon stall rates — pool walled and non-walled episodes together. A stall against an impassable facet isn't the same event as a stall in navigable vessel, so those pages need a caveat or a re-stratified rerun before they go anywhere external. The extractor already records `pl` per episode, so filtering to the passable stratum is a change in the analysis functions rather than a re-extraction.

The mechanism fits exactly, which is what makes me confident this isn't a fluke. The pair cut catheter-lead from 0.34 to 0.04 and raised stall escape from 53% to 67% — skills that pay off specifically in tight curves. The general lesson is worth carrying forward: **an intervention targeting a specific capability looks worthless when the evaluation can't exercise that capability.** Both "clean negatives" this program has produced — the reward pair and today's stochastic-eval null — were measured against a wall.

Both of your hypotheses were right, and they compound. The reward pair is a large win at *both* checkpoint choices (72.4/75.5 vs 52.0/63.3), and explore-based selection beat the broken eval by +11.3 pp for v1b and +3.1 pp for v1bp. Both true-best models now solve the CCA perfectly, 27/27.

**But there's a trade-off in the results that changes the selection advice.** v1bp's later checkpoint is better overall and dramatically better at ICA-mid (90.2% vs 63.4%) — yet **much worse at the siphon: 33.3% vs 70.0%**, 10/30 against 21/30. That's about 3 standard errors, not noise.

So v1bp's deep-navigation skill **peaked early at ~0.5M steps and then decayed** while mid-vessel skill kept climbing. Explore success% pools all depths, so it's blind to this — it picked the checkpoint that's worse at the hardest part of the task. Notably v1b shows no such trade-off (later is better everywhere), so this is specific to the reward-pair run.

That means **neither selector is adequate**: the old eval measured one tree, and explore success averages over the regime we actually care about. Depth-stratified selection is needed, or the best deep-navigation policy gets thrown away. It's the same class of error as the original single-anatomy bug — optimising a pooled scalar that washes out the thing being optimised for.

The best siphon result we now have is **70%**, from v1bp ckpt514264. That beats your historical fixed-mesh 46.2% by 24 points, on a policy that never trained on this anatomy — and against the 0/30 we were reporting a day ago.

Worth flagging for the paper: three of our recorded "results" were measurement artifacts — the 81.6% single-anatomy peak, the 35.7% real-patient row, and the reward-pair null. The two per-run PDFs still contain the refuted F2/F3 and shouldn't leave the building until corrected.

The open question I'd prioritise is why siphon skill decays after 0.5M steps in v1bp while ICA-mid improves. My guess is the same interference mechanism as F1 but at the level of task depth — as mid-vessel competence rises, deep episodes contribute a shrinking share of useful gradient. That's directly testable with depth-stratified explore success over training, using data we already have.

### Claude [223]

Both changes make the piece stronger — and the non-Markov point needs care to be technically defensible. Let me write it precisely:

Draft 3 is in [SPIE_ABSTRACT.md](SPIE_ABSTRACT.md). Prior-work framing removed throughout; the abstract now runs **gap → why this problem resists the standard formulation → why our methods follow from that → workflow → results**.

**On the technical claim — I phrased it deliberately narrower than "not Markov or POMDP", and I think you'll want to know why.** Strictly, the simulated system *is* a POMDP: the FEM state (nodal positions, velocities, active contact constraints) is Markov, and fluoroscopy is a partial observation of it. A referee who formalizes the setup could correctly object to a flat "not a POMDP" claim. So the abstract never says that. It says two narrower things that are both true and, I'd argue, stronger:

**"Not Markov with respect to the information available at deployment"** — with the physically correct hidden variables named:
- **stored elastic and torsional energy** — proximal torque doesn't transmit instantly to the tip; the shaft winds up and releases, so identical tip appearance can precede opposite tip motion
- **out-of-plane configuration** — a single projection is many-to-one
- **hysteretic stick–slip contact** — Coulomb friction is path-dependent; whether a contact sticks or slips depends on loading history, not current pose

**"The belief is not *reliably recoverable* from observation history"** — the substantive claim, and the one that does the argumentative work. Hysteresis means the sufficient statistic isn't a function of any fixed-length observation window, and the projection is non-injective. I wrote "not reliably recoverable" rather than "not recoverable" because the weaker claim is the true one and can't be knocked down by pointing at recurrent-policy baselines — of which there's a direct precedent in this exact task ([IJCARS 2023, aortic arch](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11548-023-02938-7)).

Then the third clause — **unobserved anatomy makes each vessel a distinct transition kernel** — positions it as a hidden-parameter/contextual MDP. That's the formal reason anatomy generalization is a *distributional* problem rather than a capacity problem, and it's what licenses the procedural-generation half of the paper.

Those three sentences are what make privileged training the *appropriate* response rather than one option among several: **if the belief were recoverable, a recurrent policy would suffice and the teacher would be unnecessary.** That's the logical hinge the wisdom paragraph then turns on — SOFA exposes quantities that are Markov by construction, and the planned path supplies deployable classifiers that co-vary with them, so the two navigation modes become separable.

It's 297 words, up from 254. If SPIE holds you to ~250, the compressible part is paragraph 1 — the "large sets of vessels spanning tortuosity, calibre, branch geometry" sentence can lose about 20 words without losing the argument.

\subsection{AI-generated Lung Patients with Pathology}

A Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM)~\cite{jiang2025lung} was employed to learn the distribution of three-dimensional (3D) thoracic CT volumes containing diverse pulmonary pathologies. The model was trained on intensity-normalized chest CT scans from NIH-supported cancer imaging studies accessed through the National Cancer Institute Cancer Data Access System (NCI-CDAS), including the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). Preprocessing included conversion to Hounsfield units, clipping to a lung-relevant intensity range, normalization to the model input range, lung-region cropping or masking, and resampling to a consistent spatial grid. The resulting fixed-size $512 \times 512 \times 8$ axial CT volumes were used for both model training and image generation.
The objective is to generate clinically realistic 3D lung CT volumes containing pathological findings while preserving normal anatomical structures. To achieve this, we adopt a multi-conditional diffusion sampling strategy based on iterative latent variable refinement (ILVR)~\cite{choi2021ilvr}. During reverse diffusion, the generated volume is iteratively guided by incorporating low-frequency information from multiple reference CT volumes. These reference volumes jointly constrain the anatomical structure and pathological appearance of the generated volume.
In the extension of ILVR, each conditioning reference is assigned an independently controllable downsampling factor and activation step, which determine the strength and timing of its influence during reverse diffusion. Separate reference volumes are used to guide normal lung anatomy and disease morphology, allowing the corresponding constraints to be introduced progressively during generation. By adjusting the conditioning strength and activation schedule, pathological characteristics—including appearance, size, shape, and spatial location—can be controlled while preserving the surrounding anatomical context.
This strategy enables the synthesis of anatomically consistent 3D CT volumes containing clinically meaningful findings, such as pulmonary nodules, lung masses, and other localized abnormalities. The resulting diverse pathological lung CT volumes can support downstream evaluations of CT reconstruction, denoising, computer-aided diagnosis, and virtual imaging studies.

\subsection{ CT system simulation}
To model physical particle transport and generate realistic projection data, we utilized a GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo simulation framework (\texttt{gDPM})~\cite{Jia_2011}. Phantom geometries were constructed from high-resolution volumetric CT datasets with an in-plane resolution of $0.63 \times 0.63\,\text{mm}^2$ and a slice thickness of $2.5\,\text{mm}$. Hounsfield Units (HU) were converted to mass densities and elemental material compositions following the stoichiometric calibration method detailed by Jiang et al.~\cite{https://doi.org/10.1118/1.2715481}. To mitigate axial boundary truncation and account for scatter along the superior-inferior axis, four extra CT slices were padded to both the cranial and caudal boundaries of each volume.

We simulated a helical CT acquisition with a pitch of 1, a table feed of $0.5\,\text{cm/rotation}$, and $900$ projections per $360^\circ$ gantry rotation. The simulation was distributed across six NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPUs. Projections were generated at $25\%$, $50\%$, $75\%$ and $100\%$ dose levels by proportionally scaling the incident photon fluence. The $100\%$ dose level was defined using a 32-cm polymethyl methacrylate phantom and corresponded to a CT dose index of approximately 1.5 mGy.

\subsection{Deep learning-based CT image denoising}

In this study, the flow-oriented reconstruction
conditioning engine (FORCE) \cite{FORCE_WangAXIS} is employed as a post-FBP denoising model rather than a direct projection-domain reconstruction method. The conditional model uses an EDM-based PFGM++ backbone and was trained on the Mayo Clinic public dataset, comprising 5,936 paired LDCT and normal-dose CT (NDCT) images with 1-mm slice thickness from 10 patients \cite{mayoCT}. During training, the network learns to recover the NDCT target from a perturbed version while conditioned on the corresponding LDCT image. Training involved 500,000 parameter updates on two NVIDIA A5000 GPUs and required approximately 102 hours. During inference, an initial PFGM prior is refined over 50 reverse-time ODE steps using the LDCT image as conditioning input \cite{FORCE_WangAXIS}. Denoising is performed independently for each axial slice, and the resulting slices are reassembled into a 3D volume. Because FORCE was trained on clinical Mayo data and applied to simulated FBP images, the results may be affected by cross-domain differences.
